summary: The article examines the city's Transit Authority plan, announced September 15, 2023, to make public transit accessible through low-floor buses, subway elevators, tactile paving and a new app. It details obstacles including budget shortfalls, ADA regulatory hurdles, contractor shortages, and a glitchy app, plus the impact on disabled riders and public protests demanding accountability.
one_line: The city's ambitious plan to make public transit accessible faces funding gaps, regulatory red tape, contractor shortages, app problems and public criticism.
key_facts: The Americans with Disabilities Act (ADA) of 1990 is cited as the foundation for inclusive transit, yet gaps remain more than three decades later.
On September 15, 2023, the city's Transit Authority announced a comprehensive plan to make public transportation more accessible and inclusive.
Transit Authority head Claudia Gibson called the plan "a new dawn for our city's mobility."
The plan includes low-floor buses, retrofitting subway stations with elevators, installing tactile paving, and a new app for travelers with disabilities.
Project accountant Daniel Frey said the initial budget was a best-case scenario and unforeseen costs arose, particularly in retrofitting old subway stations with elevators.
Securing additional funds has caused delays and required aggressive lobbying for more federal and state support.
City planner Helena Cho likened ADA compliance to "moving through a maze blindfolded," as every change, from door width to ramp slope, must be signed off by inspectors.
Wheelchair user Marcus Trenton said his usual station has been under construction for months and temporary access routes are sometimes inaccessible.
The accessibility app launched October 28, 2023, and has faced scrutiny for glitches and poor user-friendliness.
Visually impaired student Jessica Loomis said designers did not consult a diverse enough group of disabled users.
Chief construction officer Rick Butler called the market for specialist accessibility contractors "a seller's market," driving up costs and timelines.
Sarah Kim of the Right to Ride campaign demanded a timeline with real milestones, as advocacy groups organized protests for transparency and accountability.
